claims.text: The baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating has a nanocrystalline or fine-grained microstructure.
Controlled pre-oxidation can create an ultrathin, continuous oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
An oxidized surface layer alters dislocation nucleation during deformation.
An oxidized surface layer alters deformation-induced phase transformations.
The pre-oxidized layer modifies the surface stress state.
The oxide layer acts as a barrier to dislocation nucleation from the free surface.
The pre-oxidized layer suppresses FCC-to-BCC transformation.
The pre-oxidized layer limits abrupt or undesirable phase transformations during sliding.
Changes in nucleation sites and local strain fields produce more uniform plastic deformation.
Pre-oxidation lowers the coating's high-temperature sliding wear rate relative to an unoxidized coating.
Pre-oxidation produces more even and less localized microscopic plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
Oxidation kinetics are significant and a mechanically active, stable-oxide regime exists at approximately temperatures above 500 degrees Celsius.
The predicted improvements need not occur during ambient- or low-temperature sliding.
A controlled comparison on identical substrates under identical load, speed, and temperature can test the effects of pre-oxidation.
Failure to improve wear resistance together with failure to modify dislocation or deformation behavior would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism proposes suppression of FCC-to-BCC transformation, whereas the cited evidence reports that oxidation suppresses FCC-to-HCP transformation and instead favors FCC-to-BCC transformation.
